readonly.py:106-113 loop returns True for any token with token_type TokenType.TABLE unless previous (uppercased text of the prior token) is in _TABLE_KEYWORD_NOT_SHORTHAND_AFTER (lines 49-70). This matches the docstring at 81-85. Quoted identifiers tokenize as IDENTIFIER, not TABLE, so they are never a TABLE token. Command forms with a preceding token absent from the set (GRANT SELECT ON TABLE t, COMMENT ON TABLE t, CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE, ALTER ... ADD TABLE) return True, which the docstring says ('errs toward True', over-refusal accepted). Absolute-claim input traced: GRANT SELECT ON TABLE t has previous 'ON', not in the set, so it counts as claimed. CREATE UNLOGGED TABLE is excluded via UNLOGGED, as stated. One minor nuance: previous is matched on token text, so a quoted identifier or string whose text is 'create' or '.' also suppresses a following TABLE. No valid TABLE-shorthand query can follow such a token, so this is harmless and does not contradict the docstring's intent.

readonly.py:101-104 returns False on sqlglot TokenError; other exceptions propagate. Only two callers exist (grep of src): rls.py:228 (apply_rls) and whole_row.py:124 (_whole_row_reference). apply_rls then calls sqlglot.parse (rls.py:234-237) with the same sql and dialect, converting ParseError/TokenError to RlsError (fail closed). _whole_row_reference calls _parse_statements first (whole_row.py:121, readonly.py:642-657), which raises UnsafeSqlError on TokenError/ParseError, and also on an unresolvable dialect (ValueError). So the tokenize failure always hits a failing parse. Crafted input considered: MySQL/default dialect, where _mysql_parse_sql (readonly.py:582-639) rewrites the SQL before parse; it only replaces \r with space inside comments and raises UnsafeSqlError on backslash-escaped quotes, unterminated comments etc., so it cannot turn a tokenizer-rejected string into a parseable one (an unterminated quote stays unterminated). Unknown dialect in apply_rls: sqlglot.parse raises ValueError, which still stops the query. Claim holds.

whole_row.py:119-130 calls _parse_statements first (readonly.py:642-657 raises UnsafeSqlError on empty SQL, bad dialect, ParseError/TokenError), then raises UnsafeSqlError('empty parse tree') if any statement is None, then uses_table_shorthand(sql, dialect) returns the string 'TABLE', and only then runs the star check. So an unparseable TABLE s.t raises UnsafeSqlError from the parse, and a parseable TABLE t returns 'TABLE', which assert_no_whole_row_select (line 115-116) turns into WholeRowSelectError(WHOLE_ROW_REFUSAL), a subclass of UnsafeSqlError, with an unchanged message. tests/unit/test_safety_whole_row.py:196-212 (test_table_statement_is_refused) checks both the raise and the 'TABLE' return. Caveat: the PR removed the 'TABLE public.users' and 'TABLE app.users' cases from test_unparseable_sql_is_refused_as_unsafe, because the docs say sqlglot 30.30 and later may parse them. Those inputs are therefore refused via the shorthand path on newer sqlglot rather than from the parse; they are refused either way. One small ordering difference: an input with a None statement plus TABLE t now raises 'empty parse tree' instead of returning 'TABLE'. Both are refusals, and the docstring at lines 109-113 documents the empty-statement case.

rls.py:228-232 raises RlsError('...refusing a TABLE statement') before sqlglot.parse. The only 'could not prove' assertion (test_safety_rls.py:358) is for 'SELECT * FROM (orders) o', which is a different input and still raises at rls.py:333. test_safety_whole_row.py:204 uses WholeRowSelectError, not RlsError. test_safety_table_shorthand.py has no message assertions. NORMALIZED (wording-only): The claim misdescribes the code: apply_rls (src/sqllens/safety/rls.py:228-232) now runs uses_table_shorthand before sqlglot.parse (line 235), the multi-statement check (239) and later checks. So SQL with an unquoted TABLE keyword that used to hit a more specific error now gets 'refusing a TABLE statement' instead. Examples: 'SELECT 1; TABLE t' used to hit 'exactly one ... statement', 'TABLE public.users' used to hit the parse failure, and '(TABLE orders) sub' used to hit 'could not prove'. The PR's own tests changed their expected message from 'could not prove' or 'SELECT-shaped' to 'refusing a TABLE statement' (tests/unit/test_safety_rls.py:370-385). The message therefore does change. It is still an RlsError and the query is still blocked. The apply_rls docstring (rls.py:213-219) promises only that RlsError is raised when the statement cannot be parsed or scoped, and that promise still holds. The metadata-value checks (_resolve_value) are not reached for the cases that were already blocked at parse time. No contract, doc or caller requires the specific message to be preserved, and nothing found in the repository's rules or docs requires it either. The PR updates docs/internal/database-connectors/row-level-security.md to describe the new precedence. Every blocked input stays blocked, so no requirement is broken.

apply_rls (rls.py:228) calls uses_table_shorthand(sql, dialect) before sqlglot.parse and raises RlsError on True. uses_table_shorthand (readonly.py:73-113) tokenizes and returns True for any TokenType.TABLE token anywhere (any statement/subquery, version-independent since it does not use the parse tree), except after '.' or command keywords (CREATE, DROP, CHECK, etc.), none of which can precede a TABLE query in valid SQL (queries follow ;, (, AS, set operators, WITH CTE close paren). Absolute-claim input traced: tokenizer-rejected SQL gives False (readonly.py:103-104), but then apply_rls's sqlglot.parse tokenizes identically and TokenError is caught and raised as RlsError (rls.py:234-237), so it is still refused. Excluded-token input like 'CREATE TABLE x AS TABLE orders' has AS before the second TABLE, so it is caught. No counterexample found.

whole_row.py:119-130 _whole_row_reference first calls _parse_statements (readonly.py:642-657), which raises UnsafeSqlError('could not parse SQL') on ParseError/TokenError, so a TABLE s.t that sqlglot cannot parse is refused as unparseable. If it parses, uses_table_shorthand(sql, dialect) (whole_row.py:124) returns 'TABLE'. uses_table_shorthand (readonly.py:73-113) scans sqlglot tokenizer tokens for TokenType.TABLE anywhere (statement or subquery), skipping only after '.' or command keywords (CREATE, DROP, etc.), which are not TABLE t queries; so it is version-independent as the docstring says. Hostile input considered: 'WITH x AS (SELECT 1) TABLE t', 'SELECT 1 UNION TABLE t', '(TABLE t)' - all preceded by non-exempt tokens and refused. The unparseable sentence is conditional ('that does not parse'), matching the code path regardless of which version fails to parse it.

The diff (lines ~52-54) removes the `--constraints <(echo 'sqlglot<30.30')` line and its comment from the header; the head header (requirements.txt:6-10) recipe is now `uv pip compile pyproject.toml --universal --python-version 3.11 --upgrade --no-header --no-annotate --output-file requirements.txt`, with no constraint, so it resolves the latest sqlglot within <31 and matches the pin (30.31.0 is a valid resolution under the range).

Fixed at head. uses_table_shorthand (src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:73-113) no longer restricts TABLE to statement start or after ;, (, set operators. It returns True for every TABLE token unless the previous token text is in the _TABLE_KEYWORD_NOT_SHORTHAND_AFTER denylist (lines 49-70: '.', CREATE, DROP, ALTER, etc.). For `WITH x AS (SELECT 1 AS id) TABLE orders` the previous token is ')', which is not in the denylist, so it returns True and callers refuse it on every sqlglot version. The docstring (lines 81-91) describes this behaviour. A search of the head view for the old allowlist wording ('starts the statement', 'follows ;') found nothing, so no stale claims remain. The prior evidence's description of the check no longer matches the code.

The guard-level cases for schema-qualified TABLE are indeed absent at head: test_table_statement_is_refused (tests/unit/test_safety_whole_row.py:196-212) lists only unqualified `TABLE users`/`TABLE orders`, and test_unparseable_sql_is_refused_as_unsafe (:238-249) has no TABLE cases. The prior evidence is wrong about its consequence, though. tests/unit/test_safety_table_shorthand.py:24 asserts `uses_table_shorthand('TABLE public.users', d)` for postgres, mysql, sqlite and None. Both guards call that helper unconditionally (src/sqllens/safety/whole_row.py:124 and src/sqllens/safety/rls.py:228), and the call does not depend on whether the name is qualified. The guard tests (whole_row.py tests :208-212, test_safety_rls.py:366-385) prove the wiring, and the helper test covers the qualified-name behaviour. A regression that lets `TABLE public.users` through would therefore fail the helper test, so the finding's claim that it 'would pass the suite' does not hold. There is no criteria_file on the item, and the 'No defect' route was not used.

TABLE t`, `EXPLAIN TABLE t`) no longer holds: R_PAREN, EXPLAIN and INTO predecessors are not in the exclusion set, so they return True. The prior finding still holds at the head. src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:40-42 defines _READ_SHAPED_KEYWORDS as {SELECT, WITH, UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT, SHOW}, with no TABLE. is_read_shaped (readonly.py:159-167) is only a first-keyword membership test. Nothing in grading_rules earns a PASS: the defect is not fixed, and No defect does not apply because wrong output (a row count in place of rows) reaches the caller.
